Getting started with McBias

Ash Breidenbach

2025-09-17

The library McBias simulates and analyzes datasets using a directed acyclic graph object (DAG object) that the user sets. This allows the user to create a dataset where all effect sizes and distributions are known. By analyzing the dataset in a biased way, the user can quantify how much the biased effect size drifts from the originally set effect size.

Note: if only bernoulli or gaussian distributions are used to set nodes then the user can use the accompanying RShiny app which will write the lines of code below. In this case, skip to step 3.

You can access RShiny app url to write the code for steps 1 and 2 here.

Step 1 - Create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)

To begin we must set our DAG object with the HydeNetwork() function. Each node in the DAG will correspond to that variable’s column in the simulated datasets. Each edge (arrow) sets which nodes influence others. Our DAG object must not have bidirectional arrows or cycles. Each node in the DAG will correspond to a different column in the dataset.

#We will start with a simple DAG where node A affects node B and C, and node B and C affect Node D
#We write which variables cause others like this: 'effect|cause1*cause2*cause_n' or like this 'effect|cause1 + effect|cause2 + effect|cause_n'.
#Start each Hydenetwork argurment with ~

my_dag <- HydeNetwork(~B|A + C|A + D|B*C)

You can plot the following DAG with the Rgraphviz library if desired. Note that Rgraphviz is only available on bioconductor and can be installed as follows:

if (!require("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")

BiocManager::install("Rgraphviz")
#my_dag$dag gives adjacency matrix for plotting DAG
my_graph<-new(Class="graphAM", adjMat=my_dag$dag, edgemode="directed")
plot(my_graph)

Step 2 - Add distributions to your DAG

Once we’ve established a DAG, we must set each node’s distribution and each edge’s effect size. We can see all our node’s distributions are currently unspecified.

writeNetworkModel(my_dag, pretty = TRUE)
## model{
##    B ~ dnorm(Unspecified, Unspecified)
##    A ~ dnorm(Unspecified, Unspecified)
##    C ~ dnorm(Unspecified, Unspecified)
##    D ~ dnorm(Unspecified, Unspecified)
## }

We’ll set the distributions as follows:

  • Node A is binary, and will have a Bernoulli distribution with a probability (p) of 0.5
  • Node B is continuous and will have a Gaussian distribution with a mean of 0 and an sd of 1
  • Node C is binary, and will have a Bernoulli distribution with a probability (p) of 0.9
  • Node D is binary, and will have a Bernoulli distribution with a probability (p) of 0.25

Each interaction between nodes must have a set effect size. For this example we’ll set those as follows:

  • A -> B is 0.2
  • A -> C is 0.8
  • B -> D is 0.05
  • C -> D is 1.2

Setting effect sizes requires writing generalized linear models (GLMs) for the distribution within setNode(). First we can look up information about available distributions by referencing the jagsDists dataframe.

jagsDists[jagsDists$DistName == "Bernoulli",]
jagsDists[jagsDists$DistName == "Normal",]
DistName FnName FnNameR xLow xHigh Parameters RParameter paramLimit paramLogic Rsupport
20 Normal dnorm dnorm mu mean is.numeric(mu) TRUE
21 Normal dnorm dnorm tau sd >= 0 tau >= 0 TRUE
DistName FnName FnNameR xLow xHigh Parameters RParameter paramLimit paramLogic Rsupport
34 Bernoulli dbern 0 1 p prob 0 < p < 1 0 < p & p < 1 FALSE

Below is example code that discloses how to write them. The distributions corresponding FnName goes into the nodeType arguement. The Parameters of the distribution become additional arguments to set for the node. Pay attention to the paramLimit as errors will occur if values outside those limits are generated. Our RShiny app can write this GLM code for you as long as all nodes distributions are Bernoulli or Gaussian. Our RShiny app ensures values outside of the paramLimit will not be generated.

#we can set the distributions of each node with the setNode() command from Hydenet

#Node A is a binary variable, so its nodeType is set to "dbern" for Bernoulli. Node A is not affected by any other nodes, and thus is an independent variable. Its probability is directly set.

my_dag <- setNode(network = my_dag, 
                 node = A, 
                 nodeType = "dbern", 
                 p = 0.5)

#Node B is gaussian, so it's nodeType is set to "dnorm". It is dependent on node A so its mean changes depending on if a 1 or 0 is chosen for node A during the simulation. Since the effect size of A -> B is 0.2, we multiply that 1 or 0 by 0.2. Thus, to set node B's overall mean we take the mean, 0, and subtract it by the product of node A's probability and effect size (0 - 0.2 * 0.5).

#Since Hydenet is a wrapper for rjags, non-numeric values must be in a string, hence the paste0() function is needed.

my_dag <- setNode(network = my_dag, 
                 node = B, 
                 nodeType = "dnorm", 
                 mu = paste0(0.2," * A + ",0 - 0.2*0.5), 
                 tau = 1)

#Node C is a dependent binary variable, and thus must be wrapped in an "ilogit(" ")" command from rjags. This ensures the probability stays between 0 and 1

#Node C's overall probability is set with the set_p() function where the first argument is the overall probability (0.9) and the second argument is the product of node A's probability and effect size (0.8*0.5 for node C)

my_dag <- setNode(network = my_dag, 
                  node = C, 
                  nodeType = "dbern", 
                  p = paste0("ilogit(",0.8," * A + ",set_p(0.9, 0.8*0.5),")")
                  )

#Node D is also a dependent binary variable, so it is set similarly to node C. Note that node B's product of its effect size and mean is added to the product of node C's effect size and probability. I wrote out node B's product in set_p() for illustrative effect, even though in this case it is unnecessary because node B's product = 0

my_dag <- setNode(network = my_dag,
                 node = D,
                 nodeType = "dbern", 
                 p = paste0("ilogit(",0.05," * B + ", 1.2," * C + ",set_p(0.25, 1.2 * 0.9 + 0.05 * 0 ),")")
                 )

We can now see that all our nodes in our DAG object have a set distribution.

writeNetworkModel(my_dag, pretty = TRUE)
## model{
##    B ~ dnorm(0.2 * A + -0.1, 1)
##    A ~ dbern(0.5)
##    C ~ dbern(ilogit(0.8 * A + 1.79722457733622))
##    D ~ dbern(ilogit(0.05 * B + 1.2 * C + -2.17861228866811))
## }

Step 3 - create simulations from the DAG

Now that a DAG object is set, simulations can began. create_data() allows a single dataset to be generated. Binary nodes are portrayed as 0 or 1 integers. McBias runs its simulations inside the JAGS software. If you need to reproduce simulations, the seed must be set inside create_data() as shown. The set.seed() function in R will not create reproducible datasets.

sim_df <- create_data(my_dag, 
                      10000, 
                      seed=137 #seed MUST be set inside the create_data() function 
                      )

head(sim_df, 5)
A B C D
0 0.7441139 1 0
0 -1.2640747 1 0
0 1.6091474 1 1
0 -1.0268619 0 0
0 -0.9118822 1 0

We can check this created dataset to make sure our set distributions were set the way we expected.

Note: Bernoulli nodes that are dependent on Gaussian nodes can sometimes skew positively or negatively as their probability approaches 0 or 1 respectively. In this case, if the probability is set near 0, the generated dataset’s prevalence for the node can skew higher. If the probability is near 1 the simulated dataset’s prevalence can skew lower.

sum_df <- data.frame("Node A prevalence" = sum(sim_df$A)/length(sim_df$A),
                     "Node B mean" = round(mean(sim_df$B), 4),
                     "Node C prevalence" = sum(sim_df$C)/length(sim_df$C),
                     "Node D prevalence" = sum(sim_df$D)/length(sim_df$D))
sum_df
Node.A.prevalence Node.B.mean Node.C.prevalence Node.D.prevalence
0.503 0.0012 0.8947 0.2514

This summary of one simulated dataset reflects the distributions we set.

Step 4 - Analyze the simulations

Now that we have a working DAG object (my_dag) we can start to analyze it in various ways. varied_runs() generates multiple datasets and analyzes them as specified. It returns the summary statistics of each analysis.

Varied runs can analyze the dataset with various methods as set by the user. If this is the case, it will return summary statistics for method used. The default methods run are outlined below:

If the outcome is Bernoulli: A logistic regression is run and results are under the “regression” column. If there are covariates to adjust for, propensity score weighting is also run and results are under the “ps_weighting” column.

If the outcome is Gaussian: a linear regression is run and results are under the “regression” column. If there are covariates to adjust for, propensity score weighting is also run and results are under the “ps_weighting” column.

The user also has the option of installing matchit and running matchit analyses, as shown in the running alternative methods section.

We’ll fill in the arguments below:

  • runs = 500
    • 500 datasets will be created and analyzed
  • dag = my_dag
    • must be a DAG object
  • exposure = “B”
  • outcome = “C”
    • the datasets will be analyzed to find B’s effect size on C
  • covariates = “A”
    • A will be adjusted on
  • n = 100000
    • each dataset will have 100000 samples
  • seed = 46
    • A positive integer we can set to get reproducible results
ideal <- varied_runs(runs = 500,
                    dag = my_dag, 
                    exposure = "B", 
                    outcome = "C", 
                    covariates = "A", 
                    n = 100000,
                    seed = 46 #for seed to properly pass to JAGS it must be set within varied_runs
                    )

It returns a list with 11 elements, with each element corresponding to a different summary statistic as shown below:

  1. ratio Odds/risk ratio if applicable (will return NAs if not)
  2. calculated_ate estimated effect size/ estimated average treatment effect (ATE)
  3. lower_int lower 95% confidence interval
  4. upper_int upper 95% confidence interval
  5. p_values p_value
  6. exp_prevalence exposure prevalence, if applicable (will return NAs if not)
  7. out_prevalence outcome prevalence, is applicable (will return NAs if not)
  8. sample_population sample population
    • If matching methods are used it will report the matched sample population (i.e. if there are 10 cases in a dataset of 100, and 1:1 matching is used, the sample population becomes 20, as unmatched cases are thrown).
    • if selection bias is simulated, n will be the number of samples that entered the analyzed dataset
  9. set_ate The effect size set in the original model (considered as the true effect size)
  10. over_r the set overdiagnosis rate, if set (will return 0s if not)
  11. under_r the set underdiagnosis rate, if set (will return 0s if not)

The run results are saved as a list of 11. We can splice the results to look at any summary statistic we’re interested in.

head(ideal$calculated_ate)
##        regression ps_weighting
## [1,] -0.003515910 -0.002779031
## [2,] -0.006388331 -0.006254072
## [3,] -0.022638718 -0.022015322
## [4,]  0.003465224  0.004041182
## [5,]  0.001225602  0.001076753
## [6,]  0.001425045  0.001673759

We can visually compare the methods to each other by using ci_ridges().

ci_ridges(ideal)

We can use beta_summary() to get more details on the simulation we just ran.

beta_summary() gives the following outputs:

  • Bias and its standard error. Bias is the difference between the calculated effect size and the true effect size
  • Coverage and its standard error. Coverage gives the percentage of calculated effect sizes that contained the true effect size in their 95% confidence intervals. The aim is to have coverage be around 95%
  • Rejection rate and its standard error. Rejection rate is the percentage of times the null hypothesis was rejected as an alpha value. The alpha value can be set in the second argument and defaults to 0.05.
  • Mean B estimate gives the mean of all the calculated effect sizes.
  • B estimate std dev gives the standard deviation of all the calculated effect sizes. Provides insight into changes in precision
ideal_sim_summary <- round(beta_summary(ideal, a = 0.05), 4)
ideal_sim_summary
bias bias_se coverage coverage_se rejection_rate rejection_rate_se mean_b_estimate b_estimate_std_dev
regression 6e-04 5e-04 94.8 0.9929 5.2 0.9929 6e-04 0.0101
ps_weighting 6e-04 5e-04 94.6 1.0108 5.4 1.0108 6e-04 0.0101

So here we can see that when node A is adjusted we get a mean effect size estimate near 0 between B and C over the 500 simulated datasets. Since B has no set arc on C, the true effect size is set to 0.

ideal was the proper analysis. The collider D was not adjusted, and the confounder A was. The summary of ideal’s simulation reflects this. The difference between the mean of the calculated effect sizes and the true effect size is near 0. We also see that the rejection rate approximately equals the alpha value, which we set at 0.05. Coverage also approximately equals 95%. Overall this means that when everything is adjusted properly one gets results with very little bias, and the true effect size approximately equals the calculated effect size.

Step 5- compare multiple simulations to each other

What if the ideal couldn’t be obtained? Suppose we didn’t know to adjust for A or were given a dataset that was stratified on D? We can simulate the following scenarios to estimate how much bias different scenarios like these would cause.

  • naive: the dataset isn’t adjusted in anyway. Here we expect to see confounder bias from node A
  • selection_bias: we assume that node D represents entry into the study. We will cut samples from the dataset where D = 0 and then analyze them.
  • adjust_all: we adjust on both A and D. Adjusting on A removes its confounding, but adjusting on D creates collider bias. This demonstrates that adjusting for every available covariate may create bias.

Keeping the seed consistent across these runs ensures that the simulated datasets will be the same across the different scenarios, provided that the number of runs and number of samples are also kept the same.

naive <- varied_runs(runs = 500, 
                    dag = my_dag, 
                    exposure = "B",
                    outcome = "C",
                    n = 100000,
                    seed = 46)

selection_bias <- varied_runs(runs = 500,
                             dag = my_dag, 
                             exposure = "B", 
                             outcome = "C",
                             sb = "D",
                             n = 400000,
                             seed = 46) #n is larger here. D has a prevalence of 0.25 and only samples with D will make it to the cut dataset that is analyzed. If we want n to be similar in power to the runs we are comparing it too, we'll have to multiply n * 1/p. Keep in mind that only the first 100000 generated samples will be identical to those in the other scenarios.

adjust_all <- varied_runs(runs = 500, 
                         dag = my_dag, 
                         exposure = "B", 
                         outcome = "C", 
                         covariates = c("A", "D"), 
                         n = 100000,
                         seed = 46)

To compare these datasets with ci_ridges() and beta_summary() we can use reparse_runs(). You can use this to compare how different scenarios did. To use this, the following requirements must be met.

  • All scenarios must have the same number of runs from varied_runs(). In this example all scenarios have 500 runs.
  • The DAG object, exposure, and outcome must remain the same across all scenarios.

For this example, we’ll compare the “regression” method results of each scenario, so method = “regression”.

run_list <- list(ideal, 
                naive, 
                selection_bias, 
                adjust_all)

combined_log_r <- reparse_runs(run_list, 
                              method = "regression", 
                              list_names = c("ideal", "naive", "selection bias", "adjust all")
                              )

You can see in combined_log_r that the methods have been switched out for the different scenarios, with each run’s regression results used.

head(combined_log_r$calculated_ate)
##          ideal   adjust all      naive selection bias
## 1 -0.003515910 -0.012841010 0.03248229     0.01527533
## 2 -0.006388331 -0.014513887 0.03184389     0.03900085
## 3 -0.022638718 -0.030452852 0.01472769     0.02241356
## 4  0.003465224 -0.005170535 0.04063544     0.02072516
## 5  0.001225602 -0.006852208 0.04149136     0.01074597
## 6  0.001425045 -0.009531745 0.04000120     0.02693855

As we did before, we can use ci_ridges() for comparisons.

ci_ridges(combined_log_r, title = "Bias from Different Adjustment Sets")

As we can see, the other non-ideal scenarios show signs of bias.

We can also use beta_summary() as we did before.

combined_summary = round(beta_summary(combined_log_r), 4)
combined_summary
bias bias_se coverage coverage_se rejection_rate rejection_rate_se mean_b_estimate b_estimate_std_dev
ideal 0.0006 5e-04 94.8 0.9929 5.2 0.9929 0.0006 0.0101
adjust all -0.0080 5e-04 89.2 1.3881 10.8 1.3881 -0.0080 0.0101
naive 0.0386 4e-04 3.0 0.7629 97.0 0.7629 0.0386 0.0100
selection bias 0.0303 7e-04 51.4 2.2352 48.6 2.2352 0.0303 0.0155

All non-ideal scenarios have bias to the extent that coverage is no longer around 95%. When measuring bias it’s important to consider which impacts of it matter in your research study. We can see that the null rejection rate for all non-ideal scenarios are higher because the bias caused the mean b estimate to shift away from 0. The non-ideal scenario with the next lowest bias, adjust_all, still has a null rejection rate twice that of the ideal scenario’s.

Running Alternative Methods

Alternate regression methods

If needed, specific types of regression can be set with the family argument.

default_run <- varied_runs(runs = 500,
                          dag = my_dag, 
                          exposure ="A",
                          outcome = "C",
                          n = 10000, 
                          seed = 67,
                          family = quasibinomial(link = "logit"),
                          ) #default

probit_run <- varied_runs(runs = 500,
                         dag = my_dag,  
                         exposure = "A",
                         outcome = "C",  
                         n = 10000, 
                         seed = 67,
                         family = quasibinomial(link = "probit")
                         )

cloglog_run <- varied_runs(runs = 500, 
                          dag = my_dag,  
                          exposure = "A",
                          outcome = "C", 
                          n = 10000,
                          seed = 67,
                          family = quasibinomial(link = "cloglog")
                          )

combined_regression <- reparse_runs(run_list = list(default_run, probit_run, cloglog_run), 
                                   method = "regression", 
                                   list_names = c("Default",  "Probit", "cloglog"))

ci_ridges(combined_regression, title = "Bias from Improper Regression Fitting")
beta_summary(combined_regression)

bias bias_se coverage coverage_se rejection_rate rejection_rate_se mean_b_estimate b_estimate_std_dev
Default -0.0005 0.0031 95.2 0.956 100 0 0.7995 0.0700
Probit -0.3900 0.0016 0.0 0.000 100 0 0.4100 0.0355
cloglog -0.4868 0.0012 0.0 0.000 100 0 0.3132 0.0270

McBias will default to a logistic regression for a binary outcome and a linear regression for a continuous outcome. Since we set our GLM for outcome node C with log odds ratio coefficients and the logit linker function, the default logistic regression converges on the effect size estimate properly. Probit and cloglog do not fit properly to our simulated data so bias arises from an improper method being used.

Depending on the distributions you set for the outcome, a different regression type may needed (ex. family = “poisson” for an outcome with a poisson distribution). Certain regression types are incapable of analyzing certain outcome distributions. For example, trying to measure a gaussian outcome (like node B) with family = quasibinomial(link = “logit”) results in an error. The default regression is always the proper regression for any GLMs created by RShiny.

Matching methods through MatchIt

Matching methods are also available if the MatchIt library is installed. Matching methods are more computationally demanding than regression, especially with higher sample sizes (typically n > 10000). Keep this in mind when when setting the number. Users can set any distance method MatchIt offers with the match_methods argument. If the exposure is continuous data, the top 25% quartile will be marked as cases and the rest controls. Any unmatched data will be thrown from the set, the reduced sample size will be reported under the sample_population element in the output list.

matching_run1 <- varied_runs(runs = 500, 
                            dag = my_dag, 
                            exposure = "B", 
                            outcome = "C", 
                            covariates ="A",  
                            n = 10000,
                            seed = 10234,
                            match_methods = c("Mahalanobis"), 
                            ratio =1)

head(matching_run1$sample_population,3)
ci_ridges(matching_run1)
beta_summary(matching_run1)
regression ps_weighting Mahalanobis
10000 10000 5000
10000 10000 5000
10000 10000 5000

bias bias_se coverage coverage_se rejection_rate rejection_rate_se mean_b_estimate b_estimate_std_dev
regression 0.0017 0.0015 94.2 1.0453 5.8 1.0453 0.0017 0.0334
ps_weighting 0.0016 0.0015 94.0 1.0621 6.0 1.0621 0.0016 0.0335
Mahalanobis 0.0015 0.0043 95.0 0.9747 4.8 0.9560 0.0015 0.0957

Here we observe that the matching method is less precise than the weighting or regression methods, as its B estimate std dev is larger. This is due in part to the reduced sample size from throwing out the unmatched cases.
